title: A Quasidifferential Analysis of the Wrong-Key Randomization Hypothesis
authors: Tim Beyne, Gregor Leander, Mariia Mutkovina, and Ricardo Rodriguez Reveco
abstract:
The Wrong-Key Randomization (WKR) hypothesis governs data-complexity
estimates in differential cryptanalysis: wrong-key guesses are assumed to
behave as a random permutation would.  Exact
computation of fixed-key differential probabilities was, until recently,
infeasible.

We use quasidifferential trails to compute the exact
wrong-key distribution for the key-recovery map
\(G_{k,k'} = F_{k'}^{-1}\!\circ F_k\) in PRESENT-like SPNs.  A
mask-first reformulation exposes a Walsh--Hadamard structure; restricting the
transform to the low-dimensional support, together with SMT-guided trail
enumeration, reduces the cost: for a 16-bit toy cipher, from~\(2^{80}\)
to~\(2^{13}\); for \presentCipher, from~\(2^{192}\) to~\(2^{30}\); and for GIFT, from~\(2^{192}\) to~\(2^{32}\).

For the toy cipher, PRESENT and GIFT, the computed distribution is a
structured mixture: a large zero-probability class coexists with bottleneck
classes orders of magnitude above the random-permutation mean, and nothing lies
between them.
Such a distribution is not unimodal, so no Poisson or binomial law fits it for
any parameter and the hypothesis is formally false for all three targets.
For PRESENT, however, we show that this deviation does not affect the
security of Wang's 14-round differential attack.  We cast the computed distribution as a
structured composite hypothesis---the differential counterpart of the
random-permutation/composite-hypothesis model used for wrong keys in linear
cryptanalysis--and show that the shape of the wrong-key
distribution, not merely its mean, governs how many wrong keys survive the
key-recovery filter.  For PRESENT with Wang's
distinguisher, the structural signal is carried only by the right pairs, whose
weight is too small for the deviation to surface; the hypothesis remains a safe heuristic
in this case despite being formally false.  Our SMT-based enumeration tool is
publicly available.

Keywords: Differential cryptanalysis, Wrong-Key Randomization, Quasidifferential Trails


1     Introduction
Differential cryptanalysis is among the oldest and best-studied attack vectors against
symmetric cryptography [BS91]. Since Biham and Shamir introduced it, cryptanalysts have
examined all aspects of differential cryptanalysis: finding optimal distinguishers, proving
resistance bounds, and automating the search for characteristics. There are many variants,
ranging from impossible differential [Knu98; BBS99] and multiple-differential [BG11] to
boomerang [Wag99] and differential-linear attacks [LH94]. Despite this maturity, still
fundamental questions remain.

    One is the key-recovery phase. In a standard differential attack, an attacker uses a
distinguisher over several rounds and guesses subkeys for r additional rounds to check
for consistency between the distinguisher and the guessed keys. The standard statistical
model relies on the Wrong-Key Randomization (WKR) hypothesis: for any wrong-key
guess, the cipher behaves like a random permutation. In practice the model is applied in
a simplified form, with the probability that the differential holds fixed at 2−n for every
wrong key.


The problem: the WKR hypothesis is unverified. While the WKR hypothesis simplifies
analysis, it is rarely verified. Theoretical intuition suggests it should fail in several contexts.
For example, consider a key-recovery step with a single round. If a wrong-key guess differs
from the correct key by only a few bits, the decryption is almost identical to the correct
one, preserving the differential property with high probability (Figure 1).
   Until recently, exact verification was infeasible. Computing the exact differential
probability for a fixed key (rather than an average over all keys) was an open problem.
Standard tools only computed expected probabilities (pEDP ) over random keys, hiding
the specific behavior of individual key candidates. In the linear-cryptanalysis setting, an
analogous limitation has been addressed through composite-hypothesis techniques and the
random-permutation model for wrong keys [BR25, §7.3.3].


The solution: quasidifferential trails. Beyne and Rijmen [BR22] made fixed-key proba-
bilities expressible exactly, through quasidifferential trails. This is what lets us test the
WKR hypothesis instead of assuming it: it is a claim about the wrong-key hit probabili-
ties, and quasidifferential trails are the first general method that expresses them exactly.
Key-averaged tools such as the DDT or the expected differential probability average them
away, and direct experiments cannot measure probabilities as small as 2−n —distinguishing
a fixed-key probability pG = 2−n from pG = 0 would need on the order of 2n samples per
key. Expressing these probabilities and computing them are different problems, however:

evaluated naively, the expression is a doubly exponential sum, infeasible even for our toy
cipher. Making it computable is the technical core of this paper (Section 4).


1.1    Related work
Fixed-Key Differential Behavior. The fact that differential probabilities depend on the
specific key has long been known. Knudsen [Knu93] already observed significant deviations
from stochastic equivalence for the iterative characteristics used in the differential analysis
of DES. Experimental studies, such as those by Heys [Hey20], further showed that such
deviations are the norm rather than the exception. Daemen and Rijmen [DR07a] analyzed,
for two rounds of the AES, the case of “plateau characteristics,” which take only two possible
values per key. This line of work was recently extended by Canteaut and Fruchon [CF25]
to cover more general structures. Beyne and Rijmen [BR22] introduced quasidifferential
trails, providing the first rigorous method to compute exact fixed-key probabilities. This
technique was later extended by Boura et al. [BDG25] to cover the expected differential
probability computation, while Peyrin and Tan [PT22] investigated key dependencies to
demonstrate that valid trails can often be incompatible with the cipher’s key schedule.
Exact computation matters in practice: for the SPEEDY family, Boura et al. [BDBN23]
mounted a full-round differential attack on SPEEDY-7-192, computing the distinguisher
probability under the standard product-of-DDT heuristic. Beyne and Neyt [BN24; BN25]
later showed, using quasidifferential trails, that the main characteristic underlying this
attack has probability zero. Similarly, Dobraunig et al. [DEKM16] showed, in a practical
attack on MANTIS5, that some wrong keys are differentially equivalent to the correct
key. For PRESENT specifically, Tezcan [Tez16] showed that differential factors in the
PRESENT S-box reduce the advantage of Wang’s attack [Wan08] by a further 6 bits,
independently confirming that the attack’s key recovery is more constrained than the
nominal 32-bit claim suggests.

Statistical key-recovery models. Evaluating the success of a differential attack requires a
statistical model. Selçuk [Sel08] formalized the ranking approach, using order statistics to
estimate the probability that the correct key ranks among the top candidates. Blondeau et
al. [BGT11] later introduced the hypothesis-testing formulation, which models key-recovery
as a binary classification problem and provides accurate data complexity estimates using
large deviation theory. Both approaches heavily rely on the WKR hypothesis to model
the behavior of incorrect key candidates. While the WKR hypothesis simplifies analysis,
its validity has been questioned, particularly in the context of linear cryptanalysis, where
correlation biases for wrong keys are known to vary [BT14]; see [BR25, §7.3.3] for a
textbook treatment. In differential cryptanalysis, generic key-recovery tools like those by
Boura et al. [BDD+ 24] optimize the search algorithmically but generally operate efficiently
under the assumption that the underlying statistical model (and the WKR hypothesis)
holds.

WKR Violations in Practice. Concrete deviations from the WKR hypothesis appear
across cipher families. In Default [BBB+ 21], whose equivalent-key structure is a design
property, Nageler et al. [NDE22] exploited large classes of equivalent keys: many wrong-
key guesses produce identical differential behavior rather than the uniform distribution
predicted by the WKR hypothesis, and combining information across rounds recovered
the full key with negligible complexity. In the ARX setting, probabilistic neutral bits
(PNB) [AFK+ 08; FT25] capture a structurally analogous phenomenon: wrong-key guesses
that differ from the correct key only in neutral bit positions preserve the elevated differential
probability, creating wrong-key distributions in which a subset of keys retains a high
differential probability instead of all wrong keys behaving alike. A third class of extreme

WKR violation appears in LowMC [DEM16; LSW+ 22], where a sparse S-box layer forces
the key-recovery map onto a near-linear structure, enabling algebraic attacks that exploit
predictable wrong-key behavior. The hypothesis also fails outside differential cryptanalysis:
Todo et al. [TIM+ 18] showed that the corresponding assumption does not hold for fast

designs and that methods to compute, rather than assume, them are a necessary tool.

1.2      Our contributions
In this work, we revisit key-recovery differential attacks without relying on the WKR
hypothesis. Our contributions are threefold.

Formalization. We recast the WKR hypothesis as a falsifiable claim about the wrong-key
hit probability of the chain Fk−1 0  ◦ Ek : for k 0 6= k, the probability that a pair with input
difference a triggers the counter is distributed as it would be for a random permutation.
This fixes the whole law and not just a mean; the simplified form used in practice
replaces it by the single value 2−n . The object we compute with is the key-recovery
map Gk,k0 := Fk−10  ◦ Fk ; the distinguisher Ek0 enters through the right-pair probability pR
(Section 3.3). Quantitative wrong-key models exist for linear cryptanalysis [BT14; BR25];
in the differential setting the hypothesis is usually stated qualitatively. We state it as a
claim that can be tested cipher by cipher.

Tool. We develop a general method to compute the fixed-key probability distribution of
a differential through a keyed permutation; it may be of independent interest beyond the
key-recovery application. By reversing the summation order in the fixed-key characteristic
formula of [BR22], we expose a Walsh–Hadamard structure over the intermediate-mask
space and exploit that the relevant masks lie in a low-dimensional subspace. Combined
with an SMT-guided trail enumerator for PRESENT-like SPNs, this reduces a computation
exponential in both the state size and the number of rounds to one exponential only in
the dimension of the mask support. For PRESENT this is a reduction from 2192 to 230 ,
and from 280 to 213 for the toy cipher of Section 2.5.3

Phenomenon and model. For the toy cipher, PRESENT and GIFT-64, we exhibit the
fixed-key spectrum of Gk,k0 as a structured mixture rather than the dispersed but unimodal
law a random permutation would give. A large zero-probability class appears alongside
classes exceeding the random-permutation mean by several orders of magnitude, with
nothing in between. We compare throughout against the random-permutation model, not
against the point mass at 2−n that the standard formulas use: a point mass is refuted
by any dispersion at all, so refuting it would establish nothing. Beyond the histogram,
we identify the algebraic structure behind the partition into equivalence classes: they
arise from cosets of a vector space determined by the quasidifferential trails. We use the
computed spectrum as the wrong-key model in a composite-hypothesis test, in place of the
single alternative that the WKR hypothesis assumes. Within this model we show that the
shape of the wrong-key distribution governs how many wrong keys survive the key-recovery
filter, a quantity the mean alone cannot capture. We also identify a bottleneck class: a
small set of wrong keys whose differential probability is so high that they pass the filter
almost as often as the right key. The two are separate effects, and we compute both. A
bottleneck limits how far ranking can narrow the candidate list, while its contribution to
the survivor count depends on how many keys it holds — for our toy cipher, four. Crucially,

1.3     Outline
Section 2 fixes notation, recalls quasidifferential trails, and states the classical counter-
based key-recovery setup together with its standard Neyman–Pearson statistical framework.
Section 3 takes a closer look at wrong-key randomization: it introduces the key-recovery
map as a formal object, reviews the two pre-existing models of wrong-key behavior, states
our accurate refinement, and analyzes how the shape of the wrong-key distribution—not
just its mean—controls the post-filter survivor count. Section 4 gives the method: the
mask-first formulation, the dimension-reduction argument, the SMT trail enumerator,
and the certified mask dimensions of the three targets. Section 5 concludes with open
directions.

2.2.3    Quasidifferential trails
The sum in Theorem 1 ranges over all sequences of linear masks (u2 , . . . , ur ). Each such

transition matrix entries. When all masks are zero (ui = 0 for all i), a quasidifferential
trail reduces to an ordinary differential characteristic.

2.4     Statistical models for key recovery
Blondeau et al. [BGT11] recast the counter-based key-recovery attack as a binary hypothesis
testing problem, parametrized by two quantities: the success probability PS (the probability
that the right key is included in the output set) and the gain g (measuring the reduction
in key space). When the attack outputs an expected 2m−g candidates from a key space of
size 2m , the gain is g bits [Sel08].
    We model the key-recovery procedure by viewing the counters T (k 0 ) as random variables.
Since structured key-guessing outputs exactly the set {k 0 : T (k 0 ) ≥ 1}, the same model
applies to both approaches.
    For the right key k, the key-recovery map is the identity function, so the probability that
a pair suggests the key equals the distinguisher probability pR , the fraction of pairs that
are right pairs. We assume this is a key-independent probability.4 When the distinguisher
probability has heterogeneous behavior over keys, we are in the setting of weak key attacks.
    Hence, the counter distribution after testing N pairs follows a binomial distribution:

                                      T (k) ∼ Binomial(N, pR ).                                      (13)

2.4.1    Hypothesis testing approach
Blondeau et al. assume the wrong-key randomization hypothesis (coined by Harpes, Kramer,
and Massey [HKM95] for linear cryptanalysis and first stated explicitly for the differential
setting by Blondeau and Gérard [BG11]), and apply it in its simplified form: the differential
hits a wrong key with probability 2−n , so the wrong-key counter follows Binomial(N, 2−n ).
We call this form the point-mass simplification and separate it from the hypothesis proper
in Section 3.2; the formulas of this subsection are the ones the literature derives from it.
For each key candidate k 0 , we test

                                  H0 : T (k 0 ) ∼ Binomial(N, pR )

    In practical differential attacks, the distinguisher probability pR is typically such that
the expected number of right pairs for the correct key is small (often around one). In this
regime, keeping only the top-ranked key (ranking with r = 1) is equivalent to accepting

procedure implemented by structured key-guessing strategies. For these two reasons, we
focus on hypothesis testing throughout this work.
    Classical hypothesis tests are parametrized by two types of errors:
  • Non-detection probability PND : The probability of rejecting the right key (Type I
    error).
  • False alarm probability PFA : The probability of accepting a wrong key (Type II
    error).
   The success probability and gain introduced earlier correspond to PS = 1 − PND and
g = − log2 (PFA ), respectively.

This section asks whether a more accurate model of wrong-key behavior could prevent

We instantiate the two-stage basis search for PRESENT-like SPNs. The SMT solver

exhaustive search.

Variable encoding. A quasidifferential trail is represented by two families of bit-vector

     • Input variables (ui , ai ) for i = 1, . . . , s, where ui ∈ Fn2 is the mask and ai ∈ Fn2 is the

the backward direction (Fk−1

4.5    Performance and scope
Our implementation is available as open-source software at https://doi.org/10.528
1/zenodo.22129299 and consists of Python modules for SMT model construction, trail
enumeration, and post-processing (FWHT and Gaussian elimination for basis computation).
For the PRESENT experiments in Section 3.4, enumerating quasidifferential trails over
11,664 differential characteristics with r = 2 key-recovery rounds required approximately
8 hours on a single Intel Core i7-8665U CPU without parallelization. The dominant
cost is SMT solving during basis construction. Memory usage is controlled by processing
characteristics sequentially and resetting the solver between instances.
   Our tool is specialized for 4-bit S-boxes and bit-permutations, but the algebraic structure
applies generically. Extending to more general linear layers would require encoding the
corresponding constraints.

4.6    Scope: On-diagonal vs. off-diagonal in key recovery
The method of this section computes fixed-key probabilities for a single differential (α, β)
through Gκ . Its tractability depends only on the dimension d of the mask correlation
support, not on the specific differential.
    In the key-recovery context of Section 3.3, the on-diagonal transition (b, b) requires
computing fixed-key probabilities for one differential. For PRESENT, our SMT search
finds d = 30, giving a cost of 30 · 230 (Section 4.5).
    The off-diagonal transitions (γ, b) for γ 6= b would require fixed-key probabilities for 2n
different differentials. Even with comparable dimension reduction for each, 2n independent
searches would be infeasible. This asymmetry is handled by the residual WKR assumption.

5    Conclusion
We gave the Wrong-Key Randomization hypothesis a concrete mathematical object—the
key-recovery map Gk,k0 = Fk−1   0 ◦ Fk —and a computable quantity. Three advances made

this possible.
    First, the mask-first reformulation of the fixed-key probability formula exposes a Walsh–
Hadamard structure in the intermediate-mask space. Second, exploiting the algebraic
structure of quasidifferential trails restricts the transform to a subspace of dimension
d  (s − 1)n, reducing complexity from O(2(s−1)n ) to O(d · 2d ). For the toy cipher d = 13;
for PRESENT, d = 30; for GIFT-64, d = 32. Third, an SMT-guided two-stage basis search
makes this subspace computable for practical targets.
    The resulting wrong-key distributions are structured mixtures. For the toy cipher,
every wrong key with positive class probability pG sits well above anything the random-
permutation model expects, and by Lemma 1 the filter therefore leaves 31 times more
wrong keys than that model predicts at a threshold of τ = 1. A bottleneck class—four keys
out of 213 with pG = 0.625—behaves almost like the right key on right pairs; it contributes
little to that count, but it is what makes those four keys hard to rank apart from the
right one. For PRESENT, the subspace dimension d = 30 independently corroborates
Kumar’s observation that Wang’s attack recovers at most 30 effective subkey bits [Kum12];
the analogous bottleneck class exists, but its signal reaches the wrong-key counters only
through the right pairs, whose weight is the distinguisher probability pR = 2−62 , which is
negligible. Even at the full codebook of 263 pairs the on-diagonal structure we compute
changes the survivor count by less than 0.03%. For GIFT-64 the mixture has the same
shape, but its sixteen right-key families give ten distinct distributions, so the one an
attacker faces depends on which right key is in use—and they differ far more in shape
than in mean.
    WKR therefore remains a safe heuristic for PRESENT with Wang’s 14-round dis-
tinguisher even though it is formally false: the structured deviation is real, but at this
distinguisher probability it cannot surface. The random-permutation model still differs
from the computed survivor count, by a factor of 1.5 at a usable threshold, but that
difference comes from the dispersion the model itself carries, not from anything specific to
PRESENT. Whether it surfaces for other ciphers or distinguishers depends on the shape
of the computed distribution and on the attack’s data volume—exactly the quantities our
method makes accessible.
    These conclusions rest on treating the round keys as independent, so the classes we
compute are classes of the pair (k, k 0 ) ranging over independent round keys rather than
over master keys. For PRESENT this costs nothing: every class is realised by key-schedule-
consistent keys, each by exactly 250 master keys, so the classes, the weights ωi and the
survivor counts are the same whether the round keys are treated as independent or derived
from a master key. The mask space and its dimension d are unaffected in either case,
being properties of the round function and the linear layer rather than of the key values.
We have not checked the other ciphers, and the independent-round-key model remains
an assumption for them. For those, the key schedule is better imposed natively—as a
constraint inside the trail enumeration—than as a filter on the classes afterwards: a filter
can only discard classes already computed, whereas a constraint keeps the enumeration
from producing them at all.
    Several directions remain open. The SMT-based basis search is the runtime bottle-
